description: Learn what do property managers make and how to benchmark compensation accurately on your Mac to reduce turnover and manage labor costs.

intro: Property managers typically earn a base salary plus variable commissions, making it difficult to answer what do property managers make without a structured benchmarking process. Labor costs for management firms often reach 65 percent of overhead, meaning inaccurate pay structures directly hit your bottom line.
tldr: Property managers face high churn, with annual turnover rates reaching 35 to 50 percent in some regions.
Replacing one employee costs 50 to 200 percent of their annual salary due to lost productivity and recruitment expenses.
Generic salary surveys fail because they ignore the unique hybrid nature of property management roles.
Moving to real-time data platforms helps align pay with market reality and reduces internal salary dispersion.

blocks.text: The hidden cost of poor salary benchmarking

When you ask what do property managers make, the answer is rarely a single number. It is a mix of base pay, leasing commissions, and performance bonuses. If your compensation structure is not aligned with the current market, you will lose your best people. Replacing a manager earning 70,000 dollars can cost your firm up to 140,000 dollars. This includes the time spent recruiting, training, and the inevitable dip in service quality while the seat is empty.

Many firms rely on annual spreadsheets that are already outdated by the time they are finished. Without a clear view of the market, you might overpay for roles that do not require it or underpay for key positions. This creates an average salary dispersion of 25 percent within firms. That gap is often the primary driver of internal resentment and turnover.
Why property management salary benchmarking is difficult

The primary issue is the hybrid nature of the work. A property manager at a small firm might also handle maintenance coordination, leasing, and basic accounting. Generic salary surveys do not map well to these multi-faceted roles. When you compare a hybrid role against a standard title in a survey, the data is almost always misleading.

items: Variable pay complexity: Commissions and bonuses fluctuate based on occupancy, making base salary comparisons insufficient.
Regional volatility: Local housing market shifts impact the demand for managers faster than national surveys can track.
Role overlap: It is hard to find benchmark data for roles that combine administrative, field, and sales responsibilities.
Data lag: Traditional annual surveys cannot keep up with inflation-driven wage demands.

blocks.text: You do not need an expensive consultant to start fixing your benchmarking process. Start by shifting your focus to total rewards. Calculate the full value of the compensation package, including benefits and average commission payouts. This gives you a more accurate view of what your employees are actually taking home.

items: Audit your current pay bands: Use a simple spreadsheet to list every employee, their current base, and their average annual bonus.
Standardize job descriptions: Ensure that every property manager role has a clear list of duties so you can compare like for like.
Communicate ranges: Be transparent about pay bands. Employees who know where they stand are less likely to leave for a marginal increase elsewhere.
Quarterly check-ins: Do not wait for an annual review. Check your local market data every three months for key roles.

blocks.text: Using your Mac to manage compensation data

As a Mac user, you likely have your compensation data in Excel or Google Sheets. The key to better benchmarking is moving from static files to integrated tools. If you use an HRIS platform, check if it has a native integration with benchmarking tools like Pave or OpenComp. These tools pull real-time data, saving you from manual entry.

If you are manually updating your rent rolls or salary sheets in Excel, use the ⌘ + F shortcut to quickly find specific employee names or salary figures. This keeps your focus on the data rather than the interface.

faq.question: Why do generic salary surveys fail for property managers?
faq.answer: They fail because they do not account for the high percentage of variable pay and the hybrid nature of the roles, which often combine leasing, maintenance, and administrative duties.

faq.question: How often should I benchmark property manager salaries?
faq.answer: For high-impact roles, shift from annual to quarterly or semiannual benchmarking to keep pace with rapid regional market changes.

faq.question: What is the biggest cost of poor benchmarking?
faq.answer: The biggest cost is employee turnover. Replacing a manager can cost up to 200 percent of their annual salary due to recruitment, onboarding, and loss of institutional knowledge.
